newsitem.title: UK: New Pearson team grilled over Penguin hit.
newsitem.headline: New Pearson team grilled over Penguin hit.

text.p: Shareholders in British media and leisure group Pearson Plc demanded explanations on Friday over an accounting scam which is to cost the company 100 million pounds ($162 million).

The new Pearson board, headed by chief executive Marjorie Scardino, faced tough questions over why improper accounting at the company's Penguin USA book subsidiary went undetected for over five years.

Scardino, who took up her post in January, told the company's annual meeting that the problem centred on a single accounts receivable clerk who gave unauthorised discounts to customers for early payments. These were hidden in the accounts and only came to light earlier this year.

"As to motive, we believe that there has been some element of personal gain involved in this matter. We may be making a claim for recovery against one or more third parties," said chairman Michael Blakenham, who retired on Friday after 14 years with Pearson.
The company, owners of the Financial Times newspaper, took a 100 million pound charge against 1996 profits to cover the accounting scam.
It said the problem would cause a one-off delay in cash collection from many major north American customers, hitting cash flow in the first half of this year.
Pearson said it had discovered nothing to force it to increase the size of the provision, despite facing legal action from the American Booksellers Association.

It said there was no evidence that senior management at Penguin was aware of impropriety. But shareholders were amazed that the person concerned had got away with it for so long. "Did this woman never go on holiday?" asked one irate shareholder.
"She took rather a lot of holidays and to some fairly faraway places," replied finance director John Makinson.
Other shareholders were shocked that one person could cause so much financial damage.
"It is possible for a very determined individual to conceal an enormous ammount of improper accounting," said Makinson, adding that the book trade was "a very transaction intensive business".
Pearson said overseas profits could be hit if the pound remained strong against the Spanish peseta and the U.S. dollar.

Markets reacted calmly to the statement, Pearson shares adding 1.5p to 714p. Share analysts said there was a relief that the company had not come up with any fresh nasty surprises. ($ = 0.616 British Pounds)
